title: Wright Mounds, Montgomery County
summary: In Montgomery County, Adena people raised the three conical Wright Mounds, which the state survey calls an important place on the Adena ritual landscape.
bodyMarkdown:
In Montgomery County, Adena people once raised three conical earthen mounds. Together they are known as the [Wright Mounds](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Wright-Mounds.aspx), sites 15Mm6 through 15Mm8. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey (KAS) places them in the Middle Woodland period, 200 BC to AD 500, though Adena is often classed as Early Woodland. The survey calls their location an important place on the Adena ritual landscape.

## Who built them

The [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) flourished in the central Ohio Valley, including Kentucky's Bluegrass, roughly 600 BCE to 100 CE by one estimate. Its communities were small, mobile groups who hunted, gathered and grew early crops. They are best known for conical burial mounds and circular earthworks that served as ceremonial centers. Webb and Snow's 1945 study, *The Adena People*, drew on Kentucky mound excavations to define the culture.

## The 1937 excavation

In 1937, University of Kentucky archaeologists excavated two of the three mounds. The larger one, 15Mm6, measured 180 feet across and stood 30 feet high. It was built where several paired-post enclosures had stood. Ritual activities likely took place inside those enclosures.

No evidence showed saplings woven between the posts, so the enclosures may have looked more like standing screens than walled buildings.

The mound grew in stages. First, the builders made a log tomb for one person and covered the enclosure with soil. Each later construction phase came with more burials. Of the 21 people buried in the large mound, 14 lay in log tombs. That pattern suggests the mound was used for several generations.

Between the construction layers, archaeologists found many pottery vessels that had been broken on purpose. They suggest that Adena groups came back to the mound from time to time to reconnect with their relatives, perhaps holding feasts that ended with breaking the vessels.

The smaller excavated mound, 15Mm7, was built over a single circular paired-post enclosure in just one phase. Only two people were buried in it, so it was likely used for a shorter time. The third mound, the Greene Mound (15Mm8), was never excavated.

## A carved tablet

The large Wright Mound produced one of Kentucky's rarest kinds of artifacts. Adena people carved palm-sized rectangular tablets from shale, limestone, siltstone or fine sandstone, about a quarter to three-quarters of an inch thick. The Wright Mound tablet was found by archaeologists during an excavation.

The engravings often show highly stylized wild turkeys or birds of prey. KAS suggests these may reflect a belief in a layered universe, with the earth suspended between a sky world, linked to heavenly birds, and a watery underworld.

## Kentucky today

The [Gaitskill Mound](/stories/gaitskill-mounds-engraved-tablets/) is another Adena site in Montgomery County. KAS does not publish site locations. For other Kentucky Adena sites, see [Ashland's Adena mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/) and [Dover Mound](/stories/dover-mound-mason-county/).
